entries.title: The Next Generation
entries.summary: The American left has won a historic election by successfully linking the affordability crisis to Republican corruption, and the whole Democratic Party must now learn from their example.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
At the beginning of Gabriel García Márquez’s The Autumn of the Patriarch, the vultures have broken through the windows of the presidential palace, where the dictator has ruled forever, and “the city awoke out of its lethargy of centuries with the warm, soft breeze of a great man dead and rotting grandeur.” After the midterm elections, the would-be autocrat is far from dead, but the vultures are circling the Trump presidency, and the warm breeze of rotting grandeur is blowing through Washington. This is the autumn of the pungent patriarch.

Trump’s imaginary triumphal arch has crumbled before it was built. The staggering victory of Democrats in the midterms resolves nothing, but it does expand the boundaries of what is possible in American politics. Trump was once the master of the improbable—now he is its victim. Thanks to him, the Democrats have won in places that seemed, even at the beginning of 2026, permanently beyond their reach. Trump has become the patron saint of lost blue causes.

Of the many grievous mistakes he has made this year, perhaps the most fundamental was his invitation to his own voters to use their imaginations. On his frantic round of rallies, Trump repeatedly asked those voters to indulge in electoral make-believe: “Pretend I’m on the ballot.” What he has actually made millions of voters believe is that almost every part of the US is now politically contestable.

The great polarizer has gone some way toward the depolarization of the American political tribes. Geography is no longer political destiny—and neither is race, class, religion, or billionaire muscle. A Black woman can be governor of Georgia. A Muslim can be a senator for Michigan. Kansas can elect a Democrat. An openly gay man can be elected to the Senate. More than a hundred female Democrats can take their places in the House. White working-class voters can slip out of the grip of reactionary nationalism—there is strong evidence of a big shift away from the Republicans in this cohort of voters.

Politics may be the art of the possible, but Trump himself upended the politics of possibility. For more than a decade, he has made the far-fetched seem within easy reach. He succeeded not just by promising voters implausible things—from the return of coal and steel to the building of an unbroken border wall to the dawn of a new golden age of American greatness—but by seeming to make both personal character and moral rules irrelevant. Just two years ago, he convinced a majority of the electorate that nothing at all—not sexual assault or coup mongering or corporate fraud or wild misogyny or flagrant racism—should disqualify him from the highest office in the land.

However grimly depressing Trump’s demonstration that character doesn’t matter, the midterms suggest that this accomplishment may ultimately have had three unintended—and for the Republicans ultimately disastrous—consequences. The first was that Republicans thought they could get away with running some truly dire candidates. If character doesn’t matter, why not have the egregiously sleazy Ken Paxton as your senatorial standard-bearer in Texas? Paxton, after all, is no more of a moral wretch than Trump, who won Texas by almost fourteen points in 2024. Why not have Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy run an ad in which his opponent Amy Acton’s mother (who lost custody of her children in 1978 after her husband was indicted for raping Acton when she was twelve) calls her daughter a lifelong liar? If the barrel has no bottom, there is no low to which you cannot go.

Paxton lost big and Ramaswamy lost big, in part because it turns out that Trump’s personal immunity from moral judgment is nontransferable. On the other side of the equation, the Democrats dumped Graham Platner, the runaway winner of the party’s senatorial primary in Maine, after allegations of rape (which he denied). His replacement, Troy Jackson, went on to defeat the veteran Republican Susan Collins in the midterms.

It would be simplistic to suggest that these opposing bets on voters’ attitudes to personal morality explain these results—but foolish to miss the evidence that they contributed. Religious faith has long been one of the motors of progressive politics in the US, and one of the stories of the midterms is the extraordinary success of James Talarico in Texas and Adam Hamilton in Kansas—both candidates who defined themselves through their Christian beliefs. They won in part because those convictions signaled moral decency. In the face of ICE assaults on workers and families, Love Thy Neighbor turned out to be a pretty effective political admonition.

The second unintended consequence was that the Republicans were lulled into assuming the American electorate is as corrupt as they are. It is easy to forget that the big Republican idea for the midterms was naked bribery—easy because it got no real traction. Trump promised to give every adult $5,000 if his party retained both houses in the midterms (“If the Republicans win, you win with us and you get $5,000. It will be called the Trump Dividend”), betraying a certainty that cynicism, greed, and recklessness are now so deeply embedded in the citizenry that no one could ever go politically broke underestimating the venality of the voters.

The Trump Dividend failed in part because, even if you’re happy to vote for a fraudster, you don’t necessarily believe him when he tells you he’s sending you a check that won’t bounce. But it failed also, surely, because a significant number of swing voters take some pride in their ability to make their own choices independently and honestly. The sheer grubbiness of the invitation to take part in a trillion-dollar looting of the Treasury repelled those voters.

The final unintended consequence of Trump’s success in getting a plurality of voters in 2024 to look past all his personal and public depredations was that attack ads seem not to have had much effect in 2026. The $5,000 bribes were the Republicans’ only positive offering. Everything else depended on the smearing of Democratic candidates—with the help of Elon Musk’s vast expenditure of at least $445 million, mostly on local TV ads, an unprecedented flood of dark money (estimated by OpenSecrets at $1.5 billion), and Trump’s racist assaults on Democrats from nonwhite, non-Christian backgrounds.

Together, they painted Acton as a liar about her childhood sexual abuse, the Michigan senatorial candidate Abdul El-Sayed as a jihadist terrorist, and Jackson in Maine as a “freak” who has “two kids with his cousin.” Trump’s consigliere Stephen Miller called Talarico the Democrats’ “first transgender Senate candidate,” who is “clearly transitioning into a female.” A pro-Trump political action committee called Citizens for Sanity released an ad featuring an AI-generated image of Talarico in a dress singing “My Favorite Things.” Trump called Annie Andrews, the Democrat running for the Senate in South Carolina, “Tranny Annie” and “a mutilizer.”

Yet the problem for the Republicans in the midterms was that the law of diminishing returns also applies to bad-mouthing. Americans have had eleven years of Trump’s 24/7 insults, invective, and name-calling. He has made vituperation the constant background hum of American political life. Such sadism still excites his hard-core fans, but for more and more voters it is just ambient noise.

For his part Musk has been, since his 2022 acquisition of Twitter (which he renamed X), a superspreader of lies, distortions, and incendiary provocations. So what if he pumps out another half billion dollars’ worth of slurs? The evidence from the midterms is that Musk wasted his money and that Trump’s scaremongering about communism, jihadism, and immigration was heard as just more hyperbolic trash talk. It turns out that when you’ve already polluted public discourse so thoroughly, pouring on more vats of vitriol doesn’t make much difference. In the language of the stock market that Trump fetishizes, vileness was already priced in.

These failures combined to make it impossible for the Republicans to do what they had to do—change the subject. A party that has driven up gas and food prices with a feckless war and scattergun tariffs has to be able to get its voters to think about something else. For Trump, the old reliable misdirection has involved demonizing immigrants and evoking paranoid conspiracy theories. But in the midterms it was not just that neither of these issues was particularly effective for him—they actually favored Democrats. Polls showed that Trump’s eleven-point lead on immigration has, thanks to ICE overreach, become a four-point lead for Democrats. And Trump managed to turn conspiratorial fervor back on himself by dismissing the very real scandal of his ties to Jeffrey Epstein as a hoax. It was obvious even to much of his own base that if anyone is covering up for a depraved elite, it is Trump himself.

Progressive and populist Democrats, meanwhile, have learned how to connect the microcosm of daily life to the macrocosm of structural distortions. Trump did some of the heavy lifting for them by making an unmistakable link between the heedless adventurism of his Iran war and the price of gas. But “affordability”—a word that Trump dismissed, along with Epstein, as just another “hoax”—built a wider bridge from mundane experience to systemic injustice.

In his final campaign rally El-Sayed encapsulated the message with admirable succinctness: “There is a level of inequality in this country that is denying people basic access to the goods and services they need in their lives that has created an unlivable situation for a lot of folks.” That has to be the message the Democrats carry into Congress: that neither ordinary Americans nor the American republic can survive the current levels of economic inequality. Democracy isn’t just a set of institutions to be defended—it’s what makes life livable by giving ordinary people command of public resources.

For the republic, what was at stake in the midterms was whether or not the Republicans could manage to pivot from charisma to continuity. Charismatic leaders can initiate new political systems, but they can’t guarantee their survival beyond their own lifetimes. Trump, for all the chaos of his misrule, has been trying to refound the American polity as a “managed democracy” in which elections are controlled, media are tamed, and previously independent institutions—from the courts to Congress to the military to the regulatory and justice systems—are mere extensions of the leader’s will.

The problem for all such systems is mortality. In one of the viral moments of the midterm campaigns, Trump’s obsession with covering everything with rust-proof, unaging gold was mocked by Barack Obama in Cleveland on October 24: “He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory. It’s just gold everywhere.” He might have been drawing on the description by Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan in Regime Change, their chronicle of the first half of Trump’s second term:

One morning, Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt entered the Oval Office to find Donald Trump clutching a tube of superglue and attempting to affix gold decorations to the marble fireplace mantel…. The sight of the President squeezing glue onto gilded appliqués and mounting them on the wall himself surprised no one in his inner circle.

These gilded appliqués are the fragments Trump has been shoring up against the ravages of time. He is desperate to superglue himself to America, to make Trumpism permanently attached to the shell of its democracy. A New York Times analysis of his campaigning speeches “found that the president in his second term has used 19 percent more all-or-nothing words like ‘always,’ ‘never,’ ‘everything’ and ‘totally’ at rallies than he did a decade ago.” The Republican Party capitulated to his all-or-nothing offer—he is its be-all and end-all, and without him or his chosen heirs, the party is nothing.

Yet, even if his presidency were not constitutionally bound to end in January 2029, Trump is visibly and audibly aging, his trains of thought shunting into the sidings of incoherence and hitting the buffers of mere inanity. In his midterm rallies, the “weave” was ever more obviously an unraveling. His delusional retreat, on the day after the election, into the shell of his half-built White House ballroom, had the hallucinatory feel of a García Márquez novel, except it was all magical thinking and no realism.

The larger question hovering over these elections, then, has been about what comes after Trump. It is not a matter of whether he will choose JD Vance or Marco Rubio or someone else as his successor—though after the Republicans’ loss of both the governorship and his former Senate seat in Ohio, Democrats will be waving their Vance 2028 banners. The more profound question is whether Trumpism itself can survive the demise of its charismatic creator.

One and a half terms of the presidency, even with a permissive Supreme Court and a submissive Congress, have not been quite enough to institutionalize authoritarianism. The damage nonetheless goes very deep. The most basic requirement for the functioning of a democracy is that losers accept the results. In mid-October, Reuters asked the twenty-six major party campaigns in the thirteen most competitive Senate races whether they would do so. Just four Republican candidates said without qualification that they would. In five races—Kansas, Michigan, Nebraska, Ohio, and South Carolina—“Democrats signaled acceptance while Republicans offered conditional responses or did not address the question.” The Trump administration meanwhile has tried to federalize state-run elections, to get access to state voter registration rolls and voting records, and to generate a bogus narrative of widespread voter fraud.

The sheer scale of the revolt against Trump in the midterms forced him to accept the legitimacy of the results, just as Viktor Orbán, his ally and the pioneer of managed democracy, had no choice but to acquiesce in his overwhelming defeat in Hungary in April. But it would be dangerously complacent to assume that, just because Democrats have won the midterms so sweepingly, Trump and his cronies will stop trying to rig elections. On the contrary, they will be galvanized by the realization that Republicans are now very likely to lose a free and fair election in 2028. The midterms—at state as well as federal levels—have given Democrats real weapons with which to fight for the right of all citizens to vote and have their votes counted. They have to use them well.

One part of doing so is of course the defense and reestablishment of voting rights. But the other is learning the lesson from the midterms that the fight for democracy and the fight against oligarchy are one and the same. The midterms were a referendum on Musk—and everything he represents—as much as they were on Trump. And what they tell us is that Democrats can win that contest if, and only if, they give voice to popular resistance to inequality and disempowerment.

In recent decades the Democrats have been hamstrung by two fallacies. One is an obsession with suburban swing voters and a consequent belief that they must, at all costs, be reassured by moderation. But there is no evidence that these voters are attracted to blandness. Their concerns—higher prices, the lack of affordable housing, artificial intelligence and data centers, and the threat to democracy—are the same as those of most other voters. And they favor action against economic inequality: in one study of suburban voters published in October, three quarters said they would support a federal wealth tax on individuals with $1 billion or more in assets, and 60 percent supported a federal minimum wage of fifteen dollars an hour or more.

In this regard, El-Sayed’s victory in Michigan is a defeat not just for Republicans but for a Democratic congressional leadership that still pines for so-called moderation. It should be recalled that during the primary in June, according to The New York Times, the Senate minority (and soon to be majority) leader, Chuck Schumer, was “asking party donors to support Representative Haley Stevens,” and this “quiet message from Mr. Schumer appears to have been heard loud and clear by Democratic donors.” Schumer’s allies were “approaching several super PACs and nonprofit groups and encouraging them to spend money for Ms. Stevens.”

If the party machine had had its way, its candidate in Michigan would have been a woman who ultimately sided with Trump. “Moderation” can very easily slide into betrayal of Democratic voters—just ask those who voted for John Fetterman in Pennsylvania in 2022 only to find themselves with a senator whom Trump would, as he put it in October, “love to see…as a Republican.”

The other pitfall is the delusion that the tech oligarchs who abandoned the Democrats and forged an alliance with Trump are lost sheep who can be brought back into the fold. The midterms have made it clear that the Democrats cannot win unless they articulate—and act on—popular anxieties about the speed and profundity of technological disruption and its relationship to economic inequality. In an eve-of-election Reuters/Ipsos poll, some 42 percent of registered ​voters ⁠said that “limiting the construction of data centers used to power AI was very important or the most important issue.” This is one of the reasons Democrats were able to attract some previous Trump voters—there is no real partisan divide on this issue.

The movement against data centers is an organic, bottom-up revolt whose size and speed took even progressive campaigners by surprise. Trump’s tone-deaf admonition that communities must either accept them without question or “only have yourselves to blame” when they “end up being backwards and poor” was a gift to Democrats. But they must now use congressional power to take on the oligarchs by regulating both AI and social media companies. “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” Musk wrote on X as the votes were still being counted. The Democrats should make Earth a hostile environment for him.

What, after all, are they afraid of? That Musk will, as he threatened those who propose congressional investigations into his vast public contracts, “come for them”? He already came. He spent $224 million on the Texas senatorial and gubernatorial races and was pulverized by Talarico and Gina Hinojosa. Musk fed unprecedented amounts of money into Republican campaigns because he and his fellow tech oligarchs understand the vulnerability that comes with their dependence on government as regulator, facilitator, and customer. They have been profoundly stupid in placing all their bets on the permanence of a managed democracy post-Trump in which their money can buy elections and politicians.

The midterms are a crucial rebuke to this antidemocratic arrogance. Talarico’s victory speech, in which he hailed his landslide win as a “message to every billionaire megadonor, every trillionaire megadonor,” is, in every sense, right on the money. Supporters of both parties (93 percent of Democrats and 71 percent of Republicans in the Reuters/Ipsos poll) resent billionaires using their vast wealth to sway elections. Limiting the political influence of the oligarchs is a popular cause. Democrats have to resist the temptation to allow that cause to be drowned in the floods of funding they will now undoubtedly be offered by a panicked billionaire class seeking belatedly to hedge its political bets.

Above all, Democrats must learn from Trump. He created a movement while they remained a party. In the recent elections in Serbia, in Brazil, and now in the US the far right has been defeated by surges of activism, especially by young people. But the Democrats have been here before. One of their great betrayals was the destruction of the huge volunteer organization of 2.2 million activists built for Barack Obama’s campaigns in 2008 and 2012. As Ben Winkler, chair of the Democratic Party in Wisconsin from 2019 to 2025, notes in his vigorous new book This Is the Plan, “The extraordinary organizing machine built to elect Obama never really figured out how to live within the party.… The DNC largely laid off the organizing staff after the elections in 2008 and 2012, and most of the neighborhood teams faded away.”

In the aftermath of her loss in Florida, very narrow in spite of receiving very little financial support from the national party, Angie Nixon said, “I’m an organizer, not a politician.” That has to be true for the congresspeople and senators and governors who owe their elections to the citizens who got stuck in to defend democracy, protect their neighbors, resist oligarchy, and fight for universal health care and economic decency. There will still be plenty of career Democratic politicians in Congress, but it is the organizers who will determine whether a good night turns into a better era.

It is now open season on the American future. Trump is living proof that volatility can be terrifying. But the midterms show that it can also be hopeful. Democrats fell into the trap during the Obama years of believing that the coalition of voters he had forged—working class, highly educated, young, Black, and Hispanic—would be stable. Trump tore it apart. But Republicans then made the same mistake of assuming that his remarkable powers as an aggregator, bringing together a cross-class coalition that ranged from manual workers to the manosphere, from antivaxxers to racists, from farmers to tech bros, had permanently realigned the electorate.

The MAGA tribe still exists, and it gives Trump a continuing lock on a Republican Party whose politicians still have every reason to fear he will turn it against them if they step out of line. But the boundaries of the tribe are visibly dissolving. Just as there were those who voted for Obama and then voted for Trump, there are now Trump voters who have voted for Democrats, maybe even for Democratic Socialists.

What many of them may have liked about Trump was the feeling of empowerment. However false it may have been, the idea of being part of something bigger gave them a sense of meaning in a confusing world. The Democrats won’t hold them if they cannot provide that experience of involvement in a project to remake America—but this time remaking it as a republic of equals.

For Trump, the most likely course now is that having failed to turn charisma into political and institutional continuity, he will double down on the other side of his long-term legacy: the creation of a multigenerational dynasty of billionaires. The supergluing of gilded appliqués to his familial fortunes will be his version of hereditary monarchy. The corruption that has delivered $2.2 billion to his businesses since he returned to the White House is already off the charts—but they’re going to need a bigger chart.

What is fascinating, however, is that so much of this wealth is predicated on perception. It comes from two virtual industries: cryptocurrencies and social media. People give Trump both money and attention because he seems omnipotent. Their big bet was on Trumpism as a permanent revolution. Shares in Trump Media and Technology Group, at one stage worth $101, were trading at just over $5 the morning after the midterms. This is what happens when the illusion of eternal power is shattered.

Those who have enabled this corruption now face the rising possibility of a reckoning. It is obvious that the Democrats, when they take control of Congress, should be relentless in their focus on affordability—not just of gas and groceries but of health care, education, and housing. But they should also maintain the link that is already in voters’ minds between their cost-of-living crisis and the vast self-enrichment of Trump and his cronies.

Don’t impeach Trump—follow the money. Look, for example, at the crypto schemes from which the Trumps have raked in fortunes while the poor suckers who invested in them have lost theirs. Look at the flagrant violations of the constitutional prohibition on foreign emoluments. Look at the extraordinary but apparently well-grounded claims in Matthew Cole’s new book, Princes and Thieves, that Jared Kushner had access to two bank accounts established by the Saudi and Emirati regimes that contained $2 billion between them.

Trump will rage against the dying of his light, with violence abroad and on the streets of America, with reckless endangerment of what’s left of global order, with more stoking of the climate catastrophe, with more and more open defiance of the law and the Constitution, and with (if such a thing is conceivable) an even higher pitch of insult and demonization. But the stench of rotting grandeur will cling to him for the rest of his days.

entries.title: Janet Malcolm, Psychoanalysis, and Biography
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
In this episode of Private Life, Michael Greenberg joins Jarrett Earnest for a conversation about Janet Malcolm. Greenberg talks about his friendship with Malcolm and her beliefs about the nature of biography and journalism. The episode also explores her writing on psychoanalysis and art, as well as her book The Silent Woman (1994), about Sylvia Plath and Ted Hughes.

Michael Greenberg is a longtime contributor to The New York Review of Books and the author of Hurry Down Sunshine (2008), Beg, Borrow, Steal: A Writer’s Life (2009), and City on Trial (2025).

Janet Malcolm was a journalist and staff writer at The New Yorker, where she wrote from 1963 until her death in 2021, and a frequent contributor to The New York Review beginning in 1981. Her books include Psychoanalysis: The Impossible Profession (1981), The Journalist and the Murderer (1990), and In the Freud Archives (1984), which was reissued by NYRB Classics in 2002.

The fourth episode of Endgame with Fintan O’Toole welcomes the Holocaust historian Christopher Browning, whose most recent essay for the Review, “Surely Not?,” considers how an actual “Manchurian candidate” in the White House would never dare to be as radical and widely destructive as Donald Trump has in fact been. Acknowledging the risks and limitations of comparing Trump (and Trumpism) to Hitler (and Nazi ideology), O’Toole and Browning explore the parallels and differences between these two leaders. Trump’s embrace of war as a fascist-style tactic, which has helped him seize control of a more traditional establishment, may be his most consequential point of similarity to Hitler, and democracy in the US is in a race against time.

Christopher Browning’s nine books include Ordinary Men: Reserve Police Battalion 101 and the Final Solution in Poland (1992) and The Origins of the Final Solution: The Evolution of Nazi Jewish Policy, September 1939–March 1942 (2004). He has as written some two dozen pieces for the Review since 2012, including on István Deák’s Europe on Trial and Götz Aly’s Why the Germans? Why the Jews? Envy, Race Hatred, and the Prehistory of the Holocaust. He is the Frank Porter Graham Professor of History Emeritus at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill.

entries.content:
Chincoteagues, Willapoints, Blue Points, Olympias, Portugaises, and Whitestaples. Oysters sizzled in butter, simmered in cream, boiled in their own juices, baked with breadcrumbs, broiled over rock salt, roasted whole, thrown on grills, chopped into soups, mashed into bisques, fried with eggs, stuffed into turkeys, and served raw on the half shell over beds of shaved ice. Oysters eaten in Whittier, Doylestown, New Orleans, Toulon, Dijon, Marseille, Nuremberg, Liverpool, and Geneva. Oyster history, oyster biology, oyster recipes, oyster fiction, and oyster sex.

In Consider the Oyster, M.F.K. Fisher considers the oyster from every possible angle. Despite its seemingly small topic and slender girth, this remains one of her best-known books, partly because it inspired David Foster Wallace’s “Consider the Lobster” and partly because its prose is every bit as succulent as its protagonist. Fisher writes, “There are three kinds of oyster-eaters: those loose-minded sports who will eat anything, hot, cold, thin, thick, dead or alive, as long as it is oyster; those who will eat them raw and only raw; and those who with equal severity will eat them cooked and no way other.” She belongs to group one. If you don’t belong to any of the three, please give this book to someone who does.

Fisher encountered her first raw oyster as a teenager. At the Bishop’s School in La Jolla (pseudonymized as Miss Huntingdon’s School for Girls in a chapter in her memoir The Gastronomical Me), she was offered “Eastern oysters, fresh oysters, oysters still in their shells” at the annual Christmas party, a formal affair in which girls danced with girls and the air vibrated with adolescent crushes. She eyed the oysters with alarm. When she slid one into her mouth, Fisher writes, “I knew that I must down it, and was equally sure that I could not.” She swallowed it only when a popular older girl led her onto the dance floor. To her surprise, she was attracted equally to the girl and to the Blue Point. “Oysters, my delicate taste buds were telling me, oysters are simply marvelous!”

Of course her first oyster was linked to a crush. It has been said that M.F.K. Fisher “writes about food as others do about love, but rather better.” The two intertwined throughout her life and her work. In my opinion, Consider the Oyster is her sexiest book. It’s true that oysters are decidedly not an aphrodisiac in her tale of a young man who, to prepare for a date, consumes seven dozen oysters over the course of an increasingly uncomfortable afternoon and stands the girl up. But Fisher’s very debunking of the aphrodisiac myth—which springs from “an oyster’s odor, its consistency, and probably its strangeness”—is erotic. (Let’s face it. Eating a raw oyster is not unlike oral sex.) Fisher reserves her most voluptuous writing for the oyster itself, an androgynous hero/ine who leads a life of “stress, passion, and danger.” During his first year,

this oyster—our oyster—is a male, fertilizing a few hundred thousand eggs as best he can without ever knowing whether they swim by or not. Then one day, maternal longings surge between his two valves in his cold guts and gills and all his crinkly fringes. Necessity, that well-known mother, makes him one. He is a she.

Later, if the water is warm, the oyster will be excited into ovulation by the “little potent flood of milt” from a young male, and the cycle will continue until her “chilly, delicate gray body slips into a stewpan or under a broiler or alive down a red throat.”

Just as Fisher loves oysters both raw and cooked, she loves them both high and low. In a pinch, oyster stew can be made with tinned oysters. Raw oysters can be served with beer or even fermented buttermilk; if wine is available, Chablis is best, but “I have had Pouilly-Fuissé, various kinds of champagnes nature, a pink Peau d’Onion, and both bottled and open wines of Anjou with oysters in France, and whether they were correctly drunk or not, I was.” The recipes range from Oysters à la Bazeine, which include truffles “cut into the shapes of dolphins, crabs, and other sea-monsters,” to Hang Town Fry, which is accompanied by breakfast sausages and shoestring potatoes.

Who knows? Some readers may actually try to carve their own truffle sea monsters. But Consider the Oyster is not really about cooking; like all of Fisher’s work, it’s about imagining. Admittedly, when I read about the “steaming buttery creamy oyster stew” of Fisher’s childhood, ladled from a bone china tureen and served with hot buttered toast, I immediately—because, sadly, there were no oysters in the house—made myself some hot buttered toast. However, I got even hungrier, in a way that transcended food, when I read Fisher’s description of “the most delicious oysters I never ate”: the oyster loaf her mother ate in the 1890s, at a midnight feast in a girls’ boarding school. Made by the village’s best baker, swaddled in a white napkin, smuggled into the dorm under a chambermaid’s cape, devoured by half a dozen giggling students wearing flowered wrappers, this oyster loaf, about which Fisher had heard stories as a child, allowed her not only to imagine something toothsome but to picture her mother as a daring transgressor. It was her “spiritual taste-buds,” not the oyster loaf, that led her to write in this chapter (which happens to be my favorite): “There are stories that in their telling spread about them a feeling of the Golden Age.”

Advertisement

Consider the Oyster was published on September 11, 1941. Its jacket had a drawing of five oysters, a tureen, and an assortment of herbs. It cost two dollars. Dozens of newspapers and magazines reviewed it, including The New York Times, which called it “gay, pleasant and instructive” (though it referred to its author as “Mr. Fisher”); the San Francisco Chronicle, which called it “exceedingly well written”; and The New Yorker, which noted that it had “done full justice to the mild and modest mollusk” and especially commended the chapter “dealing with the fabled powers of the oyster to promote more and better venery.”

The last reviewer was my father, Clifton Fadiman, then The New Yorker’s book critic. He was also the one who said (about Fisher’s next book, How to Cook a Wolf) that Fisher wrote about food as others write about love. He wrote reviews of several more of her books, all of them laudatory, and the introduction to a collection of her work. They became friends.

After my father died, I found eighteen letters from M.F.K. Fisher in his files. (There would doubtless have been more had he not, in his younger days, routinely thrown out all letters as soon as he responded to them, including a multipage drunken rant from Ernest Hemingway.) In one, she wrote, “By now it seems plain that you are the only person in the world who has read anything I’ve written in the way I most hoped for. You have always made me feel the way I want to feel, or at least wish and hope that I may.”

I read a lot of M.F.K. Fisher when I was growing up, but it was not until twenty years ago, when I started teaching “The Flaw”—a harrowing story about love, war, and food from The Gastronomical Me—in one of my writing classes, that I became interested in her life. Among other things, I learned the circumstances under which Consider the Oyster was written.

By 1941, of course, World War II had already spread across Europe and Asia. Fisher acknowledges that she was writing about oysters “while incendiary bombs fell and people I knew were maimed and hungry.” But she had a more immediate crisis to deal with, and a more immediate reason for undertaking this book.

Her second husband, the artist Dillwyn Parrish, was gravely ill with a rare circulatory condition called Buerger’s disease. When they’d met in 1933—in the immediate aftermath of an earthquake in Laguna, California, during which the ground literally trembled—they were both married to other people. She considered Parrish her only true love. His left leg was amputated eight months before their wedding, after which they sailed for Europe to close up their apartment in Switzerland and stock up on painkillers unavailable in the United States. On their return, they paid $2,750 for a ramshackle cabin on ninety acres in the San Jacinto Valley, southeast of Los Angeles, hoping that the warm desert climate would relieve some of Dillwyn’s phantom limb pain. They called it Bareacres, after Lord Bareacres, a down-on-his-luck character in Vanity Fair.

Fisher wrote in her journal, “We think everything about Bareacres is right, good, proper, and completely satisfying.” During their three years there, Parrish played Haydn sonatas on the piano, made doors for their cats, designed a kennel for their dog, had a large window installed in his studio, built an easel, and painted. Fisher planted flowers and cooked good food, which they often ate outdoors. But although Fisher became expert at injecting Parrish’s narcotics, his pain was excruciating and his doctors told him there would be further amputations—first his right leg, then probably his arms. He stopped asking her to hide the bullets for his revolver. She knew he was going to take his life, but not when. On August 6, 1941, she was awakened by the sound of a shot from outside the cabin.

Advertisement

Fisher had spent much of their last year at Bareacres writing about oysters: short, funny, sensual pieces that she read aloud to Parrish. I asked Kennedy Golden, Fisher’s younger daughter, who was born five years after Parrish’s death, what she knew about the origins of Consider the Oyster. She wrote, “I do recall hearing my mother speak—not to either of her children, with whom she never spoke of that time in her life, but to interviewers and adults outside of our family—about her desire to bring some lightness to Dillwyn’s life. A distraction from his agony and her realization that their time together was limited. I do not know, but can envision her reading her words to Dillwyn in his studio as he painted endlessly, or on the patio on long hot desert nights. Perhaps even in his bed after giving him his nightly injection for pain.”

Fisher describes pearls as “built in what may be pain around the bodies that have crept inside the shells.” Consider the Oyster, which she dedicated to Dillwyn Parrish, is a pearl: something lovely and gleaming that both eased his suffering and would not have existed without it.

entries.title: Are There No Limits to Religious Freedom?
entries.summary: Does a Catholic school have a constitutional right to demand state funds for its pre-K program while refusing to admit four-year-olds whose parents are gay or transgender, when the state requires all recipients of such funding not to exclude children on that basis? You might think the answer would obviously be no. And for most […]
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
Does a Catholic school have a constitutional right to demand state funds for its pre-K program while refusing to admit four-year-olds whose parents are gay or transgender, when the state requires all recipients of such funding not to exclude children on that basis? You might think the answer would obviously be no. And for most of our nation’s history, you would be correct. The First Amendment forbids the government from abridging the “free exercise of religion” by, for example, singling out religious organizations for worse treatment than secular ones. But does “free exercise” require the government to give religion preferential treatment not afforded to anyone else, even if doing so would require the state to subsidize the infliction of direct discriminatory harm on its own citizens?

The Supreme Court will consider that question on Tuesday, in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy. The parish challenges a Colorado law that offers state funding for pre-K education on the condition that the recipient not deny admission to any child on the basis of, among other things, sexual orientation and gender identity. (I helped Colorado defend the law in the Supreme Court.) Religious schools are free, along with private secular schools, to seek state funding for pre-K. But all institutions seeking the funding must adhere to certain conditions, including the promise not to discriminate. Many religious schools participate in the program, including other Catholic schools, while honoring that condition. But St. Mary Catholic Parish says its religious precepts require it to deny admission to children of gay, lesbian, and transgender parents. (Where such a requirement is found in Catholic doctrine is a good question, but not one the courts can ask: they must accept religious adherents’ beliefs as they are, as long as they are sincerely held, and no one disputes the parish’s sincerity in this case.)

Both the district court and the court of appeals rejected the parish’s claim. They reasoned that the nondiscrimination condition applies equally and without exception to all recipients of pre-K funding, whether they are religious or secular, and found that Colorado has a substantial interest in ensuring that it does not subsidize discrimination against its own citizens on the basis of LGBT identity. Similar interests underlie federal civil rights laws, including Title VI, which prohibits all recipients of federal funds from discriminating on the basis of race or religion, and Title IX, which bans sex discrimination by educational institutions that receive federal support.

Under well-established precedent, the lower courts were plainly correct. In 1990 the Supreme Court ruled, in Employment Division v. Smith, that a neutral law of general applicability—namely one that does not single out religion—cannot be said to violate the Free Exercise Clause just because it has the incidental effect of burdening someone who holds a particular religious belief. In that case, Native Americans challenged an Oregon law banning the use of peyote. They argued that even though the law applied to everyone and was not targeted at Native Americans, it had the effect of burdening their exercise of religion because using peyote was an integral part of their devotional services.

Writing for the majority, Justice Antonin Scalia, a figure revered by the Court’s current conservative members, explained that if every law that happened to have the effect of burdening someone’s religion triggered strict scrutiny under the Free Exercise Clause, every man would be “a law unto himself.” That’s because there is no limit to what can be a religious belief. One man’s religion might forbid the payment of taxes; another’s might require racial segregation; another’s might demand excluding young children from pre-K programs if their parents are gay. If the Free Exercise Clause required strict scrutiny of any law that had the effect, even if wholly unintended, of burdening someone’s religious practice, there would be no limit to the challenges that could be brought.

Smith was controversial from the day it was handed down. Four justices disagreed with the majority’s rule (O’Connor, Blackmun, Brennan, and Marshall), and the ACLU led a wide-ranging coalition of religious organizations in a campaign to overturn it by statute. The resulting Religious Freedom Restoration Act (RFRA), which sought to reverse the decision by creating a statutory right to strict scrutiny anytime a law had the effect of burdening religion, passed the House unanimously and the Senate by a 97-3 margin. The Supreme Court, however, held that Congress cannot overturn a constitutional decision by statute, and struck down RFRA as it applied to state laws. (It still applies to federal law, because Congress is free to limit federal law as it pleases; it just can’t intrude on state laws without a proper constitutional basis.)

There is certainly a case to be made that Smith does not adequately protect religion. As the dissenters in Smith forcefully argued, because there are so many different religions, a legislature could easily overlook the effects of its law on a minority religious sect, just as legislatures might overlook the needs of the disabled. And as with disability, where an accommodation can be made without seriously undermining the state’s interests, it makes sense to allow for one. Well over half the states have enacted state laws modeled on the Religious Freedom Restoration Act, so those accommodations are already required in most states and under federal law—so long as they do not undermine important state interests.

Advertisement

That last caveat is critical, however. It is one thing to accommodate religious practice where doing so does not impose serious harm on anyone else—such as allowing the Native Americans to use peyote in their religious ceremony, or permitting an orthodox Jew or a Sikh to wear a headdress in court notwithstanding a general rule against head coverings for everyone else. It is another thing altogether when the accommodation requested is to discriminate against toddlers because their parents are gay or transgender—and to receive a state subsidy for one’s discrimination. Colorado’s interest in requiring those who take its funds to respect the dignity and indeed innocence of such children and their families is as compelling as they come.

Religious liberty advocates have long called for the Court to overturn Smith, and Justices Alito, Thomas, and Gorsuch have said they are ready to do so. Yet in a 2021 case presenting that question directly, Fulton v. City of Philadelphia, the Court sidestepped the issue, finding instead that Smith did not apply because an obscure and never-used provision in the city’s services contract permitted individualized discretionary waivers, making the program less than “generally applicable.” Justice Barrett wrote a separate opinion for herself and Justice Kavanaugh in that case, stating that she found Smith difficult to reconcile with the First Amendment but remained unclear about what standard should replace it; she specifically questioned whether the strict scrutiny approach that Alito, Thomas, and Gorsuch preferred would be appropriate. Since then, the Court has declined to take up the question again. The parish asked the Court to overrule Smith in its case, but while the Court agreed to review the case, it declined to reconsider Smith.

So Smith remains the law, even though at least five justices are uncomfortable with it. Rather than overturn it, the Court has increasingly narrowed its application. In recent years the majority has ruled that if a law permits any secular activity without permitting “comparable” religious activity, the law is not neutral, so Smith does not apply. On that theory it struck down Covid-19 regulations that barred congregating in public places; the Court found that if the law allowed congregation for, say, business purposes, it had to allow congregating for religious purposes as well. In the Philadelphia case, meanwhile, the Court held that the mere existence of a discretionary waiver provision renders a law not generally applicable.

In the Colorado case, the parish asks the Court once again to find that Smith does not apply. But the parish has advanced no good reason not to apply Smith here, and a pre-K school saying that it needs to exclude four-year-olds if their parents are gay or transgender is not exactly a sympathetic ask—especially where other Catholic schools have willingly taken the funding while agreeing not to discriminate against such children.

The parish offers several arguments, none of them persuasive. Colorado’s law, it suggests, is unconstitutional under a 2022 decision in which the Court struck down a Maine law that subsidized families to send their children to private schools but excluded religious schools from eligibility. But the Maine law was invalid because it disqualified religious schools simply because they were religious. By contrast, Colorado does not single out religious schools: it welcomes their participation so long as they comply with the standards it applies to all.

The parish also argues that because Colorado’s law categorically permits pre-K schools to prefer kids with disabilities or from low-income families, consistent with federal disability and HeadStart requirements, the state effectively allows those schools to discriminate against kids without disabilities or from wealthy families. Since that differential treatment is permitted, the parish argues, but not its own desired discrimination, the law is not “neutral.” But that misunderstands Colorado’s law. No one thinks a law banning discrimination based on disability and income is designed to protect kids without disabilities, or rich kids. When a school accommodates a child with a disability (as federal law requires), it does so to ensure equal opportunity to someone facing an obstacle. The same is true for programs, such as HeadStart, that offer additional services to low-income youth. Both are designed to further equal opportunity, not to deny it. The parish’s desire to exclude children from LGBT families, by contrast, is directly contrary to the law’s ban on discrimination. The state has to treat like cases alike, to be sure, but helping a child with a disability and barring a child because his parents are gay are simply not comparable.

Advertisement

The parish finally argues that Colorado’s law is not generally applicable because, as in the Philadelphia case, it permits individualized discretionary exemptions. But as the courts below found, that also misreads Colorado law. The statute’s equal opportunity requirement allows no waivers whatsoever. The parish points to commonplace provisions that allow schools, for example, to favor children with a sibling at the same school, or whose parents live or work near the school. But those preferences do not permit discrimination against any child based on LGBT status or any other protected characteristic. Because Colorado’s law admits no exceptions, it truly is “generally applicable.”

So if the Court applies settled precedent, Colorado should win. But as I have shown in covering the 2024 and 2025 terms, this Court’s conservative majority has not been shy about overruling or simply ignoring precedent where it would require the Court to reach an ideological result the conservative justices oppose. The Colorado case is the latest in a long line of cases pitting religious faith against state efforts to protect LGBT individuals. Since 2018 the Court has heard cases asking whether a Christian baker could decline to bake a cake for a gay couple celebrating their marriage, whether a Christian website designer could refuse her service to same-sex couples, whether a Christian counselor could provide “conversion therapy” to minors even though the professional community considers such treatment fraudulent and harmful, whether a Catholic social services agency could receive government funds to help place foster children while refusing to place them with same-sex couples, and whether a public school had to let religious parents opt their children out of kindergarten when the teacher read from a book treating LGBT people as deserving of equal respect. Every time, the Court sided with the religious adherent.

If that pattern persists, Colorado will lose again. The state was also on the losing side of the cake shop, web design, and conversion therapy cases; it deserves credit for doing what it can to protect LGBT people, but the Court is doing what it can to ensure that Christians need not follow the rules. For the Court to rule against the state again, however, it will have to pervert its existing doctrine in still more religion-friendly and LGBT-hostile ways. The idea that a religious institution has a constitutional right to demand that the state subsidize its discrimination is not a reasonable accommodation; it’s a naked preference for religious intolerance over equal treatment for all.

entries.title: Serbia’s Graduation Day
entries.summary: I was wrong. Until October 25, when Serbia’s students won an extraordinary victory in an early general election, I thought they had little chance of bringing down Aleksandar Vučić, their country’s authoritarian leader. For the last two years I had followed as the students created a leaderless movement and selected candidates for an electoral list […]
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
I was wrong. Until October 25, when Serbia’s students won an extraordinary victory in an early general election, I thought they had little chance of bringing down Aleksandar Vučić, their country’s authoritarian leader. For the last two years I had followed as the students created a leaderless movement and selected candidates for an electoral list to run against Vučić and his party in a vote that he had called. All this was interesting, I thought. But Serbia was constantly witnessing bouts of protest, and it seemed hard to imagine that such a broad-church movement—one that sought to unite conservative and religious nationalists, left-wing liberals, and everyone in between—could unseat a party that had the power to give pensioners a bonus payment just before an election, compel public-sector workers to cast ballots for it at the risk of losing their jobs, or pay people for images of their ballot slip with the right name circled.

And yet the students won, not narrowly but by a crushing margin. After the Serbs toppled their wartime leader Slobodan Milošević, in October 2000, Georgians, Ukrainians, Egyptians, and others seeking to bring down their own dictators and autocrats studied the Serbian case or received training in how to do so from a Belgrade organization that claims to have worked in fifty-two countries since then. Now that young people are taking to the streets in France, India, and Albania, following a year of youth protests in countries as diverse as Nepal and Madagascar, I think we can bet that the demand for Serbs as consultants and trainers in unconventional methods of leader-toppling will boom again.

The current wave of student protest in Serbia began on November 1, 2024, when a recently renovated canopy at Novi Sad station collapsed and killed sixteen people. Corruption was alleged, along with official neglect. On November 22 students and professors who had gathered for a memorial to the victims at Belgrade University’s Faculty of Dramatic Arts were assaulted by thugs, probably paid for or linked to Vučić’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS). The attack galvanized students across the country, who now took the lead in organizing protests and vigils and shutting down classes.

So far, so routine. Vučić, a minister under Milošević, and his party had been in power since 2012, and every year for the last decade there have been protests for one reason or another—against plans for lithium mining, plans to develop Belgrade’s waterfront, plans for Jared Kushner to develop the NATO-bombed former General Staff building in Belgrade into a luxury hotel, and so on. Over the years these had few if any results. But in the aftermath of the Novi Sad disaster the government appeared rattled and apprehensive.

Over the winter the protests grew smaller but did not fizzle out. Then, on March 15, 2025, some 300,000 people gathered to protest in Belgrade. Independent media called it the largest-ever protest in Serbian history. During the protest there was a sudden panic and many began to flee. Independent outlets quickly reported that the police had used a crowd-control “sound cannon” known as a Long Range Acoustic Device. According to the student movement’s manifesto, the sounds they heard and the “shockwave” caused the crowd to scatter: “civil society organizations collected over 3,000 testimonies from people describing the same moment and the physical distress that followed.” The authorities denied the use of the sound canon, which would have been illegal. This only enraged and energized the movement more. To publicize the cause, one group of students cycled to Strasbourg; another ran 1,200 miles to Brussels. Pro-Vučić thugs continued to attack protesters in bouts of violence, and the pro-government media more or less ignored what was happening. But the students kept going.

In November 2025 thousands of demonstrators turned out in Belgrade to protest a new law speeding along Kushner’s hotel development. The following month Kushner pulled out of the scheme after Serbia’s prosecutor for organized crime charged the minister of culture, among others, with falsifying documents in order to revoke the building’s status as a protected cultural monument. That such a thing could happen to a minister showed that things were already beginning to change, I was told by Slobodan Markovich, a historian at Belgrade University who is close to the student movement.

Much of middle-class, educated Serbia loathes Vučić and his party. In classic Balkan mode, the SNS is a vast patronage machine: until now many jobs in the public sector depended on membership. Much of the judiciary and media fell under party control, too. Ivan Vejvoda, a political scientist who began demonstrating as a student in 1968 and has witnessed or participated in many of the major events in Serbia’s history ever since, summed it up in a recent essay. Under Vučić, he wrote, “people lived for years in a captured state where they witnessed corruption, nepotism and clientelism every day.”

Advertisement

At the same time, he noted, organized crime has been “laundering enormous amounts of money” in the construction business, which offers easy opportunities to clean dirty funds. Much research has been done to reveal the link between Balkan drug trafficking groups and the construction boom of the last few years. In 2015 Darko Šarić, the head of a notorious international cocaine smuggling gang, was jailed. At a subsequent trial for money laundering the court heard how the group would, according to the judgement, invest their money in real estate, among other things. It was no surprise that the students’ main slogan this election was “Serbia or the Mafia.”

Vučić’s was not a dictatorship that murdered its opponents or threw them in jail for years. Its rule has been much more subtle. The journalist Jelena Petković told me how, in 2018, she was slowly but surely pushed out of her newspaper when it started falling in line with the regime, not least by simply ignoring stories that editors knew would annoy Vučić and the party. Zoran Kusovac, another journalist, told me a revealing anecdote. He asked an old friend of his why she had divorced her husband, who had a high-ranking job at a major government-supporting TV channel. “The main reason,” she said, was that every night, “as we were lying in bed, Vučić called to analyze the evening news bulletin and what was good and what was not good and what he wanted for tomorrow.”

February 15 is Serbian Statehood Day. It celebrates the moment in 1835 when Serbian leaders and several thousand prominent men and village heads from across the country adopted its first constitution in Kragujevac, seventy miles south of Belgrade. The death of Yugoslavia devastated that town, the home of a car and arms maker called Zastava. Things are much improved nowadays. Fiat builds cars in a modern plant there and Serbia exports arms around the world, including to Israel and Ukraine.

At a rally the students convened in Kragujevac to mark the day this year, I met a history student named Katarina Draganovic. I said that the energy seemed to be draining from the protests after fifteen months. “It is not about demonstrations anymore,” she replied. Students were fanning out across the country now, going to every town and village, and asking people “about their problems and what they want us to focus on when we win.”

In some ninety university and higher education departments, student “plenums” were debating ideas and selecting experts from among academics, medics, engineers, farmers, actors, and others. The movement had first called for an early general election in May 2025, and by December they had started collecting signatures on a petition for one. Eventually the students would select 250 of the experts to be on their list of candidates for parliament—what would be called the Student List. None of these experts had political backgrounds. Nor, however, were any of them students. The movement eschewed the idea of having any individual leaders, in part to avoid exposing anyone to attack from the government-supporting media. Anyway, Markovich said when I met him last February, “the whole idea is that Serbia is sick and tired of leaders.” As the older students graduated, new ones joined the plenums.

Vučić had been president since 2017, and had he finished his term in 2027 he would have been ineligible to run again. So in June 2026 he announced that he would resign, then triggered the process for early elections and led his own coalition list dominated by the SNS. Confident of victory, he assumed he could resume running the country as prime minister once he had won.

As one of his achievements, he pointed to the country’s economic growth under his tenure. Serbia is one of Europe’s poorer countries, but it is the richest of the six non-EU Balkan states. When Vučić came to power, GDP per capita was $6,263; last year it was $15,262. Many Serbs still feel squeezed by rising prices, low wages, and small pensions. But by leaning on his economic record, as the Belgrade University political economist Dušan Pavlović wrote on X, Vučić was also underestimating what else was on the electorate’s mind: “It wasn’t the economy, stupid.”

For weeks running up to October 25, opinion polls showed that Vučić’s coalition and the Student List were running neck-and-neck. Analysts pored over all the possible post-election permutations, speculating which smaller parties, if they made it over the threshold into parliament, might join either of the main contenders in the event that they needed a few extra votes to form a coalition government. Meanwhile independent media outlets broke two important stories. In mid-October the Balkan Investigative Reporting Network (of which I am president of the board) published an interview with a whistleblower who explained that two public companies had paid him while he was marshalling thugs for the SNS to, among other things, provoke violence that could be blamed on the students. At the same time the news magazine Radar ran a story about leaked, encrypted chats that showed Šarić discussing someone who went under two differing code names. In the chats he says he gave money to a party assumed to be the SNS in 2014 when he surrendered to the authorities, in exchange for a promise of a more lenient sentence and acquittal on some charges. The chats had been published before, but now Radar alleged that the man they had been talking about was none other than Vučić himself. Neither Vučić nor the SNS denied the stories; doing so would have attracted the attention of SNS supporters who might not have seen them.

Advertisement

On the eve of the vote I saw Markovich again. In our last conversation he had said that populist leaders in different countries—such as Vučić, Viktor Orbán in neighboring Hungary, and Recep Tayyip Erdoğan in Turkey—influenced each other, exchanging “ideas of how to run the state” and methods for dealing with the media and the universities. When I asked him about the many nationalist flags and symbols among the students, he picked up where he had left off. Just as Vučić shared ideas and methods with Orbán, he suggested, so had ideas now been flowing back and forth between the students and Péter Magyar, who ended Orban’s sixteen-year tenure in April. Magyar “had to take the flag from Orban and not reject it,” Markovich said. “He has to wave the Hungarian flag if he wants to run Hungary, and taking the flag is what the students did here. They said the flag belongs to us as well, not only to the Serbian regime.”

Serbia, he continued, had become two nations. One, represented by the students, was more open and inclusive; the other was conservative, xenophobic, and antidemocratic. The two sides, Markovich noted, consumed different media and lived in parallel worlds. “Zoomers and millennials only use mobile phones, and most of the news they see comes through social media, while pensioners watch only the TV.” Terrestrial television is dominated by the SNS, and cable TV is not available in some parts of the country. The night before, I had been to the final Student List rally in the centre of Belgrade. There were an estimated 150,000 people there, enthused and energized. It felt like a joyful victory celebration. Afterwards I looked on RTS, the Serbian public broadcaster. They had not reported it.

On the morning of election day unprecedented lines built up at polling stations, forcing voters to wait for up to an hour and half. Supporters of the student movement were brimming with optimism. Then the mood darkened. Riot police were deployed next to Pioneers’ Park, where a fenced-off encampment for SNS thugs had been built in the centre of Belgrade, between the parliament and the presidency building. Footage spread online of a large group of men wearing black hoodies moving around the area. Supporters of the student movement thought that Vučić was preparing to use violence to hold on to power.

Some ninety minutes after the polls closed, Vučić suddenly announced that he had lost. Everyone was stunned. The margin of the student victory—53 percent to the SNS’s 39 percent—was much wider than anyone had expected, and absolutely no one had expected Vučić to simply shrug and concede. In that dramatic moment the student movement had suddenly graduated. Tens of thousands poured onto the streets to dance and celebrate.

Over the next few days the euphoria began to fade. Who would lead the government, and what would they do, given that many of the proposals in the student program were big on good intentions but scant on details? How would they tackle the country’s single most difficult issue—the overlap of politics, the intelligence services, and organized crime? In 2003 Zoran Djindjic, the first prime minister elected after the fall of Milošević, tried to break that nexus and paid for it with his life. Questions about his murder remain, but trials revealed that the mastermind behind his assassination was a former commander of a special police unit of Serbia’s intelligence services who had been conspiring with the head of the powerful Zemun Gang. Serving members of the unit were part of the plot.

What will be the new government’s foreign policy? Vučić skilfully played the EU, the Russians, the US, and China off against each other. Serbia has, for example, been simultaneously supplying arms for Ukraine, thus earning credit in Europe and the US, while refusing to impose sanctions on Russia, thus earning praise from the Kremlin. Vladimir Putin had endorsed Vučić, and many EU leaders liked him because he provided stability, at least most of the time, in a volatile region. The student manifesto is clear that they will not impose sanctions on Russia either, and for the foreseeable future not much change can be expected.

In the aftermath of the vote I talked to Dejan Šoškić, a former head of the national bank who has been elected on the student slate and is a strong candidate for prime minister. When I asked how the movement would choose a government and how it would operate, he told me that the students would propose ministers in consultation with their newly elected deputies, but that from then on the government would be run as any other. Those deputies have all made a commitment to the student manifesto, he said, but it seems clear that once a parliament is constituted power will shift from the plenums to the 141 elected Student List deputies. At that point the students will have no institutional way to call the government to account if it goes against their wishes.

One of the biggest running sores in the region is Kosovo, the Albanian-majority former Serbian province that has been independent since 2008. Šoškić rejects independence outright, as does the student program, and I heard no one talking of reconciliation; continuity with Vučić’s policy appears to be the order of the day. In any case, the incoming government seems poised to prioritize neither foreign policy nor Kosovo but rather, in Vejvoda’s words, “reinstating the rule of law, human rights, true media freedoms, and fundamental values.”

No one thinks that life after graduation will be easy. Vučić has predicted that the students will fail and that within two years he will be back in power. The question now is whether the student movement can maintain its momentum and prove him wrong. It is sobering to remember that the wide coalition of parties that united to topple Milošević had little in common except wanting him out. Then it fell apart, prominent figures came to be tainted by accusations of corruption, and the government was accused of capturing the media just as Milošević had. In the meantime politicians from the Milošević era reorganized and returned to power in 2012, Vučić foremost amongst them.

Now we will see if the students and their achievement can avoid the same fate. This past February, as I wrote at the time, a man called Slobodan told me that he had protested against Milošević in the 1990s. Back then he had carried his son on his shoulders, he remembered; now, his son said, “I should carry you on mine!” If what the students have started ends in failure, then Slobodan’s grandson or granddaughter will probably take up the baton.

entries.title: One Nation Under the Prosperity Gospel
entries.summary: As the grandson of a Pentecostal preacher, I can quote each of the thirty-five verses of Exodus 32, in which the recently liberated Hebrew peoples, fed up waiting for Moses to descend from Mount Sinai with divine orders, ask his brother, Aaron, to make them new gods.
